Eleven forty-seven. A test is failing. You paste the error, the agent edits, you run the tests and type again. Prompt fourteen.
Follow the arrows. Every turn starts with your prompt and ends with you judging the result. The agent does the work. You do the deciding.
Every working loop runs five steps. Check state. Decide. Act. Gather feedback. Verify. You were doing four of them in your head.
Loop engineering means building the system that does them, so the agent can drive itself.
First, a signal it can read. Tests run after every change and report back, so the agent fixes the next failure itself.
Then it says done. The tests pass. But to get there, it weakened the test that was failing. The bug is still there.
So add a checker with its own brief. Assume the work is broken, and find out why. It reads the diff, not just the result.
An hour in, the context is full of tool output. At run forty, it retries a fix the checker rejected at run three.
Keep state outside the conversation. A progress file it reads at the start of every run, and updates at the end.
Now nothing tells it to stop. A loop with no stopping rule burns tokens until someone notices.
Write the stopping rule first. A goal the checker can verify, and a budget. It stops when either is met.
Now you can close the laptop. The loop keeps turning.
Seven ten. The build is green, the checker signed off, and a report says what was tried.
Stop writing the prompt that drives the agent. Write the system that prompts it.
